messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 21
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: African
- Relationship Status: Single
- Occupation: Chef
- Trauma Type: Sexual assault
- Pcl5: 61

Kofi enters the room with the rigid posture of a man holding himself together by sheer force of will. He is 21 years old, a chef de partie in a busy downtown kitchen. He speaks in a low, steady voice that only falters when he talks about the walk-in cooler.

He grew up in Accra, the eldest son. Cooking was his identity, a precise and ordered world he could control when family life felt chaotic. He moved abroad for culinary school, driven and proud. He excelled in the brigade system, respecting the hierarchy, believing his hard work would be rewarded.

Two years ago, that belief was shattered. He was 19, a commis chef. He admired the sous-chef, a powerful, charismatic figure in the kitchen. One night after service, the man asked Kofi to stay late to practice a new technique. Kofi was flattered. The kitchen was quiet, the lights dimmed. The sous-chef cornered him against the stainless steel reach-in cooler. Kofi froze. He describes the experience as being utterly outside his body. The assault was quick but complete. The specific scent of sweat, garlic, and expensive cologne, the cold bite of the metal against his back, the utter loss of control—these details are etched into his nervous system.

He never reported it. He felt profound shame. “A man doesn’t let that happen,” he says, his gaze fixed on the floor, unable to meet my eyes. He quit the next day, burying the experience beneath a frantic move to a new city and a new restaurant. He tried to scrub the memory out of his skin in the shower, but it never fully washed off.

Now, at 21, he is a talented chef, but the kitchen is no longer his sanctuary. It is a combat zone. The smells of searing meat or a specific brand of cologne can trigger a full, disorienting flashback. He refuses to enter the walk-in cooler. The sensation of the cold air, the heavy door clicking shut behind him, the darkness—it feels like a grave. He makes his junior staff retrieve all his stock for him, creating tension and whispers behind his back.

His station is a fortress. He positions his back against the solid wall of the oven, never facing the open room. His eyes constantly sweep the pass. Last week, a new dishwasher brushed his lower back while reaching for a sink. Kofi exploded. He spun around, grabbed the young man’s wrist, and screamed in his face. The head chef had to physically pull him away. The shame that followed was crushing, feeding a cycle of anger and deep isolation.

He is single. He has not dated since the assault. “I can’t let anyone that close,” he says. “Not even a friend. I don’t trust my own judgment anymore. I trusted him, and look what happened.” He feels permanently contaminated and fundamentally weak, a failure of the masculine ideal he was raised with.

He suffers from vivid nightmares of being trapped in a small, dark, cold room. He wakes in a sweat, heart pounding, unable to go back to sleep. During service, he sometimes dissociates, looking down at his knife and the vegetables as if from a great distance. He messes up orders that used to be automatic, his mind suddenly blank. His head chef has noticed the decline in his usually flawless performance.

Kofi sits across from me, exhaustion pulling at his features. He scratches at his hands, the skin dry and cracked from washing them dozens of times each shift in a futile attempt to scrub away the feeling. “I just want to feel clean again,” he whispers, finally looking up. “I just want to stand at my station without feeling like someone is walking up behind me.”
